title: What Have You Been Watching? (Week of (February 25, 2024)

commenti.body:
The Zone of Interest by Jonathan Glazer (5/5)


It's been 2 hours since i watched it but still amazed at how this movie could squeeze you and became such a pshycological torture for everyone who watched it. The sound design is so creepy and haunting. This could be a masterpiece for ages

Watched Zone of interest, amazing study on the banality of evil, subtle and efficient.The ending was superb.

Also Joaquin Phoenix is my favourite actor and he proved once more that he's one of the best of his generation.

**Ben-Hur (1959, William Wyler) — re-watch** — Better than I’d remembered it being. *Ben-Hur* is so famous for its awe-inspiring spectacle, and especially its legendary chariot race, that its takes some effort to look past that and notice how well the story at its foundation holds up. It’s no surprise why this is more-or-less the only one of Hollywood’s Bible epics that people still watch today. (Well, there’s also *The Ten Commandments*, but I already said my piece on that in an earlier thread.)

In his later years, Wyler reportedly often remarked that it took a Jew to make a good movie about Jesus. I assumed that was just a silly joke when I first heard about it, but on this viewing I started actually gets at a deep insight into why this movie works so well. The trouble religious art so often runs into is that storytellers instinctually want to make their own religion seem *obviously* true and good, and in so doing make the stories behind them seem pointless — if Christianity really were obviously true, how could it take an infallible deity to come up with it? The preaching works for Wyler because he’s able to convincingly portray what hearing the Gospel is like from the perspective of someone who genuinely struggles with its teachings — not out of malice or stupidity, but simply because it’s alien to his ingrained view of the world.

I came very close to giving this a perfect score, but a few minor issues hold it back. First, romantic subplots were almost always the weakest part of Old Hollywood epics, and this is no exception; that it here begins as a slave falling in love with her master is already uncomfortable enough even without Haya Harareet’s utterly worthless performance (a notable outlier among an otherwise solid cast, including possibly the best performance of Charlton Heston’s career). Also, I was a little confused as to why everyone was apparently allowed to go in and out of the leper colony whenever they wanted (it seems to defeat the purpose of having one).

But given how long this movie is, it’s pretty remarkable how few of these missteps there are. Definitely a must-watch. **9/10**

I’ve made some harsh comments about the French New Wave movement in the past, but after revisiting two of their most famous films this week, I’m beginning to come around on them:

**Hiroshima Mon Amour (1959, Alain Resnais) — re-watch** — This one went down in my estimation a little on re-watch. I had forgotten how hard I found it to take much interest in the star-crossed lovers element of the story, which takes up a pretty good chunk of it. That said, I still think this is a very good movie, and it’s one of the few French New Wave films that I’d say comes close to earning its reputation. It’s at its most effective and memorable moments when it works as a meditation on the horrors of war, but even the weaker parts are made watchable by how hauntingly beautiful the cinematography is. Highly recommended. **8/10**

**The 400 Blows (1959, François Truffaut) — re-watch** — *The 400 Blows* has long been a movie I wanted to like more than I did. I felt like I understood why so many people loved it, but something about it left me cold. It’s taken a while, but I think the movie has finally managed to click with me.

I think the biggest reason I wasn’t able to connect with this movie for so long is because of how subdued it is. I generally like dramas to be full of big emotions, which isn’t typically how Truffaut operates. But I now think this subdued style is precisely what makes this movie so remarkable. The typical approach with coming-of-age stories like this is to indulge in sentimentality, either of nostalgia or else of self-pity. Truffaut’s approach is made so fascinating because his attitude towards the troubles of his childhood self (or more precisely, his stand-in for his childhood self) is little more than a kind of detached amusement.

This applies mainly to the first two acts. In the third act, the movie starts becoming a lot more emotional, and without spoiling anything, it’s jarring in the best way. I did start to wonder towards the end whether Truffaut was spending a little too long twisting the knife, but when I got to that gorgeous final shot, I knew it couldn’t have gone any other way. Perfection. **10/10**

I’d hoped to close off this week by reviewing the Human Condition Trilogy as a block like I did with the Apu Trilogy, but I hadn’t realized how long they all were, so for now I’m only covering the first one:

**Human Condition I: No Greater Love (1959, Masaki Kobayashi)** — I was worried it might be hard to fairly judge this movie on its own, given that the trilogy was originally supposed to be one nine-hour movie. Fortunately, this first third is still brilliant enough to work on its own.

While WWII and the Holocaust are among the most common subject matters in film, the atrocities of the Japanese Empire have gotten comparatively little attention, so it’s good to see a movie that portrays their cruelty so unflinchingly. Kobayashi skillfully walks a difficult tightrope, avoiding both the risk of injecting false nuance and also the risk of turning the Japanese army into caricatures — he leaves no doubt that the policies of the Empire were indefensible evils, and neither does he ever bring into question that those who carried them out were heroes in their own minds. Easily one of the most effective anti-war movies I’ve ever seen. **10/10**

**Movie of the week**: *The 400 Blows*

watched dragnet girl (5/5) and cat in the hat (3.5/5)(2003) last few days, then seventh seal (4.5), oz (5), wild at heart (4), and moonstruck (3.5) before a trip situated in the middle of the week! 
dragnet girl somehow ended up making it up there amongst my favourite yasujiro ozu movies, somehow blending his styles and classic slow roll into a really emotional noir, with a lot of thematic content that almost seems akin to breathless in a lotta regards!

Oz and wild at heart were the same day, with wild first, and as great of a film as that was, much more importantly I finally got oz, it’s themes finally hitting home for me as an adult man. Really powerful stuff, I almost cried and it just felt really familiar and comfy, yet telling me something completely new! 

Finally seventh seal was really wonderful, my first bergman, and really really something wonderful, had me thinking for days about so much of its imagery and theming!

Sexy Beast - After seeing Zone of Interest, Jonathan Glazers' early films are getting more exposure so I'm finally completing his filmography. Under the Skin is an all-time favorite. And Zone of Interest, I will have to rewatch at some point (as hard a sell as that is), because it felt like a very objectively perfect project, like a piece in a museum, but I did hold some reservations with the experience it provides me as a film. Anyway, Sexy Beast was a lot of fun, another example of 'first films by favorite directors' where it's very solid but kinda small-scale, using a genre like crime film as a backdrop more than showing a fully amazing or unique work. Like Thief in the post-Tarantino era, I like the absurdism and humor brought to it. Amazing performances, as any review will tell you. The most easily rewatchable. 7/10

Birth (2004) - The last Glazer. Weird that it also feels like a proto-coming into his own film, but tonally I think it's more in line with where he was heading. Birth works very strongly on an emotional level. It takes you on a ride where so many questions never get answers, and so much is ambiguous. Yet the journey into illogic is thought-provoking and subversive. Kidman is the one actor made for this role, so getting her was a no-brainer but good for Glazer; she's fantastic in this. The child actor is just ok; you can tell he's directed in a way that doesn't require a rare child acting talent, but if anything that hinders the film, as ideally, some inspired casting choice could've elevated the illogical duplicity of his character and created a more flexible script. 7/10

Rear Window - I'm catching my Hitchcocks at about a 1 per year rate, and idly landed on this because I was feeling low-risk; with all I've heard of it I'm sure it will be really great. And it lands pretty immediately as a 'they don't make em like this anymore' type movie. Crowd-pleasing and expertly crafted, but with a deeply woven thematic substance. The meta and voyeur ideas translate 100% to today's time, even as the story is delivering this immersive slice of a 1950's New York summer. All the main actors are charismatic. Grace Kelly is inhumanly desirable (and someone kept getting Vaseline on the darn lens in all her solo shots), and James Stewart talks the way Nic Cage does now. As a no-frills thriller, it could be a solid 9/10. But hot take, it dragged out its runtime, and the ending was kinda anticlimactic, in the sense it drops its thematic explorations and suspenseful possibilities for the simplest of its forms. 8/10

Deadstream - completely random pick for a quick, fun watch, which it was. I admire that we have a submission in 'streamer' horror that feels like a future cult film and crowd-pleaser in the subgenre. It actually replicates the whole vibe and feel of the dirtbag 'prank'/stunt streamer well, so its satire can work. Overall the viewing experience holds up on the comedy and the horror, as you observe this character study of an attention-junky sociopath in his lane of pandering to children, and wait for the 'turn' to happen in this creepy haunted house. And things get very unambiguously violent and messy when its time to. The main actor works in 'streaming mode', but his weaknesses become apparent when he's supposed to actually be in fatal danger; it feels like he's pretending all the way to the end, when it would clearly be better to have his real character become exposed as streaming becomes less of his objective. It leads you to think the ending will be more meta than it is, which it isn't, sadly. 7/10

I’ve been going through some suggestions I found on a r/simpleliving thread, so I went to see Perfect Days yesterday and really enjoyed it. Take Joy! The Magical World of Tasha Tudor was another good find.

I’ve also been going through Adele Exarchopolous filmography, starting with Sibyle, Passages and Zero F*cks Given. Loved her in all three.

**Week # 164:**

🍿  

*"Rudy calls me The Queen Of Auschwitz"...*

After waiting for many months, I finally had a chance to watch Jonathan Glazer's transcendental **The Zone of Interest**. It's the most spine-chilling horror film I've ever seen, and one that will probably grow to become one of the greatest films of all time.

Making art about genocide is nearly impossible. Few Holocaust movies were able to tackle the topic honorably (Claude Lanzmann's epic Shoah', and Alain Resnais's 'Night and fog', both documentaries). But fictional dramas about concentration camps and Nazism are usually an affront against humanity. This one is different: Restraint, oppressive to the bone, ambient, extraordinarily disturbing. **9/10.** 

🍿  

**2 with Swedish actress Lena Olin:**

🍿 Another film about the holocaust. **One life** is the directorial feature film debut of James Hawes, who directed two of my favorite 'Black Mirror' episodes ('Hated in the nation' and 'Smithereens'). Anthony Hopkins plays Nicholas Winton, who saved the lives of 699 Czech children by transferring them to England, just before the beginning of World War 2.
 
Watching Hopkins is always a delight, but unfortunately much of the film is a historical flash-back, a genre I dislike in principle. But even as much as I can't stand the period posturing and sub-par acting in the flash-back, the pathos and manipulation used here were so effective, it left me in tears for most of the film. **8/10.**

🍿 **The Adventures of Picasso** is a Swedish surrealist comedy, very much in a 1970's absurdist style. Including a few lovely scenes (A dubbed Rossini duet, violinist Henri Rousseau ascending to heaven to the tune of 'I dream of 'Jenny', an excessive cauliflower farting performance) among mostly low-brow and stereotypical caricatures. Woody Allen did it better in 'Midnight in Paris'. 2/10. 

🍿 

And a third movie about related topic, **Hitler Lives** - 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qEYeJKCFQgA Wow! A virulent anti-German propaganda film, originally written by Dr. Seuss and directed by Frank Capra, but which was remade by new director Don Siegel, and even went on to win the 1945 Oscar. Commissioned by the War Department, it was so over the top, that even George Patton walked out of the screening for top military brass, calling it 'Bullshit'.

['Today I learnt' that Don Siegel directed his first two movies in 1945, this and 'Star in the Night', and both of them won the Oscars, one for Short drama, and one for Short documentary!]

🍿 

**River**, my second charming comedy by Japanese director Junta Yamaguchi (after his original 'Beyond the Infinite Two Minutes'). Like the previous one, it's a quirky "2 minute time loop" story, where every 2 minutes, time rewinds and everyone returns to where they were before. It takes some getting used to, but it's more relaxed [maybe because the location is a traditional inn, 'Ryokan', in a beautiful rural area]. The dozen participants adjust their responses to the Loop, and are behave accordingly. 100% on Rotten Tomatoes.

🍿 

**2 Korean police thrillers:**

🍿 **Cold eyes** (2013) is about a team of surveillance officers tracking a gang of highly-sophisticated criminals. Excellent fast-action, cat and mouse plot (with improbable tech). 6/10.

🍿 **The Outlaws** (2017) is a fast action, brutal story of a gang war in seedy Chinatown in Seoul. Tough as nails and hard hitting, the captain in charge of the investigation goes against one of the most ruthless screen villains I've ever seen, a loan shark who likes to chop people's hands off. Lead officer Ma Dong Seok is relentless and uncompromising, and with the most powerful knock-out punches. The all-out brawl at the airport bathroom executed as well as the fight scenes from 'True Lies' and 'Terminator 2'. 

The film was a big success in Korea, and they already made 3 sequels to it. **8/10 - My most entertaining surprise film of the week!**

🍿 

*"Something is rotten in the State of Denmark".*

Laurence Olivier's brilliant adaptation of Shakespeare's **Hamlet**, the first British film to win the Oscar for 'Best Picture'. It got everything: A son avenging the murder of his father, a ghost story, incest and madness, suicide, poetry, politics of the day, as well as stunning photography in German Expressionist style. Also, a 'foppish courtier', tight tights for the men and giant protruding codpieces. 

I wish I was much more versed with Elizabethan English, so that I could enjoy it even more. 

🍿 

**Marlene Dietrich as a conniving murderess X 2:**

🍿 First watch: **Witness for the Prosecution** (1957), a terrific Billy Wilder drama with Charles Laughton and Marlene Dietrich, and with Tyrone Power in his final role. My dislike for pompous courtroom dramas was surpassed by the wit and fluidity of the Agatha Christie story. **8/10.** 

🍿 The 1950 **Stage Fright** was a mediocre Hitchcock Noir, with a similar set up, featuring a conspiring, duplicitous Marlene Dietrich as a remorseless co-conspirator to a murder. Not as engaging, or as staged. The most memorable performance in it was the 'Laziest Gal in Town' scene
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5AD_Igguubk, which was parodied so well by Madeline Kahn https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9pJESEpEPlI . 3/10. 

🍿 

**Re-watching 'Singing in the rain' X 2:**

🍿 Another frequent re-watch: Nancy Meyers perfect feel-good hug, **The intern** (2015). Meyers directed only 7 movies, but wrote nearly 20 romantic blockbusters. She's a superb screenwriter, and this is a marvelously-constructed bonbon. De Nero is super cute, and even Anne Hathaway is wonderful here. The relationship between them develops in stages so well. And it culminates with the heart-warming You Were Meant for Me https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p6-j3IxQyj0 scene at the Mark Hopkins Hotel. **10/10.**

It's amusing to think how different this movie will be if Michael Caine and Tina Fey (or Reese Witherspoon) would play in it, as originally planned. That would actually be a good project for a 2026 A.I. "Alternative Version" re-make! ♻️

🍿 So I had to watch **Singing in the rain again**. If there ever was a perfect musical, this is it. There isn't much I can say that hadn't been said before many times, so here:

- The 'You were meant for me' scene which is the emotional center of the movie, happens (as it often does in Hollywood classics) at the 48:25 mark, precisely one hour before the end.
- Gene Kelly wears this ridiculously-giant white chapeau. I don't even know what it's called.  http://areyoukarl.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/31.-Gene-Kelly-Debbie-Reynolds-Singing-in-the-Rain.jpg
- The musical numbers are composed of mostly very long shots, with few, nearly invisible, cuts!
- Debbie Reynolds was only 19 when she was cast as Kathy Selden.
- And, Clockwork Orange's Alex DeLarge definitely altered forever any connotation to the beauty of 'just singing and dancing in the rain'...
**10/10 - will watch again.** ♻️

🍿 

**Once Within a Time** is Godfrey Reggio's 8th experimental feature. Like his famous Koyaanisqatsi trilogy, it's an abstract non-linear montage, but this time with a different element of story-telling, that of children watching today's world disintegrate. 

With a Philip Glass score (once again), exec-produced by Steven Soderbergh and with a cameo by Mike Tyson (?). It's a psychedelic, surreal trip, with animated dreamscapes, like La Planète sauvage on digital Psilocybin. 5/10. 

🍿 
  
"Today I learnt" about Stig Anderson, "The fifth ABBA". He was their promoter, manager, lyricist and manager. **Stikkan** is a new Swedish documentary about one of the most fascinating and influential people of Swedish music. (Even though the narrator has a very irritating intonation!).

🍿 

*"Obviously, Jesse is Tom and we're all Greg's"...*

From Southbank Central, A fascinating panel discussion with Jesse Armstrong and four other **brilliant writers of 'Succession'** on September 15, 2023. 8/10. On YouTube -  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ngzYTh02EAk

🍿 And just to follow up, I revisited 'Succession' masterful 'Pilot' episode, **Celebration**. Directed by Adam McKay, it introduced all the unpleasant main characters in such a way that one is being lured to obsessively follow them for 40 additional hours. It's also obvious from the very first viewing of Kendall Roy, with his sloped shoulders and forlorn sad-dog looks, is a 'Loser' who'll never be able to fill his father's big shoes. 10/10. ♻️

🍿 

*"I like your hairstyle... I like your polyester look"...*

When **Saturday night fever** first opened in the 70's, I was a film snob and refused to see it. After stumbling upon the iconic opening scene today, I though I'll give it a another shot. But Tony Manero still was a strutting, empty-headed, raping asshole, and the rest was not for me either. "Rocky but for Disco"? I saw Rocky recently and it was a great story. This was a ridiculous, sexist, stereotypical chauvinist, and pathetic ride. And was there a Ron Jeremy cameo? **1/10.**

🍿 

*“I’ll be watching you, al-jazeera..”*

Where do I even start? **Poultrygeist, Night of the Chicken Dead** is a piece of low-budget Troma schlock full of absurd, tongue-in-cheek body-fluid gore, the kind of shitshow I usually avoid. I thought I'll be able to see how bad can it really be, but after another explosive diarrhea gross-out scene that lasted for 2 or 3 minutes, I had to give it a permanent pass. 'Bye, Lloyd Kaufman. 1/10 - didn't finish.  

🍿 

**This is a Copy / Paste from my tumblr where I review films every Monday. 

https://tilbageidanmark.tumblr.com/tagged/movies**
I'm also a big Adele Exarchopolous fan, and am going through her complete filmography...

**The Haunted Palace (1963)** \- It's a fine but forgettable adaptation of Lovecraft's "The Case of Charles Dexter Ward". 

**Them! (1954)** \- A good idea with good execution for the time. 

**65 (2023)** \- Kind of an inverse Predator movie. Not great, not terrible, it's exactly what it looks like and does nothing that's not expected from it. A huge issue that disables it from being a bit better is that the mystery gets ruined as soon as you look at the movie poster or the title sequence of the movie >!which explains that the movie takes place on earth right away.!<

**Leave No Trace (2018)** \- A fine drama which is worth a watch, but nothing extraordinary

**Poor Things (2023)** \- I loved it. Ever since I've read The Island of Dr Moreau by H.G. Wells I was craving a good contemporary adaptation that's taken out of the era where it was written. Wells had an ambitious vision about good old victorian surgery where he explained us how any biological function can be reproduced with surgery. Poor Things scratched the itch perfectly with a unique story weaved into a beautiful cinematic experience. I loved it very much.
